extracted.intended_audience: Authors and peer reviewers using the F1000Research platform (prospective and current authors; invited reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on F1000Research's fully open, post-publication peer review model, including reviewer roles, required author actions (reviewer suggestions), approval statuses, and how articles are assessed and indexed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review model characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Our peer review process is formal, invited, and fully open (meaning the reports are published alongside the article, along with reviewer names and affiliations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review reports and reviewer names/affiliations are published alongside the article to ensure transparency and accountability. The model is designed to make peer review a constructive, collaborative conversation within the research community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of review — post-publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review takes place after the article has been published openly on the platform, so your research can start being read and used while expert reviewers assess it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because review is post-publication, articles are immediately discoverable and citable; reviews are added later as formal reports. This accelerates dissemination while preserving quality checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer role — assess quality and validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to assess the quality and validity of the research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should focus on scientific validity and methodological soundness. F1000Research explicitly welcomes null and negative studies and expects reviewers to evaluate them using the same standards as other results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article types that are peer-reviewed (and exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: F1000Research publishes a range of research outputs, which are all peer-reviewed except for Editorials, Posters, Slides, and Documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other article types (e.g., Research Articles, Software Tool Articles, Data Notes) undergo the same open, post-publication peer review process. Authors should check the article-type rules to know whether their submission will be peer-reviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval status definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles are labelled with statuses: Awaiting peer review; Approved; Approved with reservations; Not approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awaiting peer review: label applied immediately upon publication. Approved: reviewer asked for few or no changes. Approved with reservations: reviewer believes the article has academic merit but requires a number of small changes or significant revisions. Not approved: reviewer considers the article to have fundamental flaws; the article remains published and authors are strongly encouraged to publish a revised version addressing specific concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passing peer review — criteria for indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: An article passes peer review with two Approved ratings, or one Approved and two Approved with reservations, and will be included in PubMed, Scopus, and other major indexes, along with its review reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing and formal 'pass' status depend on the combination of reviewer ratings. Authors should aim for the combinations above; if Not approved ratings are given, authors are encouraged to submit revised versions addressing reviewers' concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author requirement to suggest reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Before publication, authors must suggest at least five potential reviewers who meet our basic criteria (and must continue to suggest names until at least two peer review reports have been published).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are responsible for proposing reviewers; the Editorial team will support if authors struggle to find reviewers. Suggestions should meet the journal’s basic criteria (expertise, independence) and authors must keep suggesting names until two reports are published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer diversity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s important to think about the diversity of your suggested peer reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reviewers from different institutions, different countries, and ensure a good gender balance. If the five names provided aren’t sufficiently diverse, the Editorial team may ask for more suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical tips for finding reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Top tips: Use your knowledge of the field to identify possible reviewers at relevant institutions; try the Reviewer Finder Tool; look at your references — authors of cited papers could be well-placed to review for you; explore academic databases like PubMed or Scopus for recent articles with relevant keywords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should combine personal knowledge, tooling (Reviewer Finder), citation lists, and database searches to build an initial list of potential reviewers. The Editorial team can assist if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency as a quality and accountability principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency in the peer review process is a hallmark for quality and accountability, making it easier to know if research can be trusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: F1000Research argues that open reports reduce bias, enable community conversation, improve quality (evidence that open reports tend to be more constructive), allow learning from reviewer feedback, and empower authors to lead the process by suggesting reviewers themselves.
